extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of Renaissance/medieval natural philosophy, medicine, theology, and classical learning (readers of Latin treatises)
extracted.subtask_description: Extract and analyse prescriptive and evaluative criteria found in a Latin natural-philosophical/theological treatise (discussion of societies, miracles, city-siting, human proportions, generation, upbringing, physiology).

rubrics_metrics.name: Signs and prodigies as indicators of rise or fall of kingdoms
rubrics_metrics.description: Regna, provincias et principes sunt notae et signa ac prodigia in eorum interitu ac ortu; such portents are observed and collected as evidence in the study of the fortunes of realms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observe extraordinary signs and prodigies around births/deaths/changes of rulers or provinces; such phenomena were taken as important evidence for the health and destiny of polities (the text treats collecting and interpreting these signs as an important care).

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity as prime driver of invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Human nakedness and vulnerability produced necessity, which in turn produced invention (speech, hands, arms, food, ships, instruments) — necessity forces the mind to contrive means of protection and perfection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating origins or causes of technologies or institutions, privilege explanations that trace them to practical needs (defence, subsistence, transportation) and progressive refinement by intellect and manual skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religious truth: testimonial/historical testimony
rubrics_metrics.description: One foundation for Christian claim: the careful testimony and recited accounts of what happened in Christ's time (testimonium / recitation of events) such that they are not merely proclaimed but repeatedly recited and testified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess a religion's claim partly by the reliability, multiplicity and character of recorded testimony and whether contemporary witnesses and tradition preserve a coherent narrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religious truth: miraculous evidence and its comparability
rubrics_metrics.description: Miracles are advanced as proof of a religion, but must be compared: Christian miracles (e.g., Lazarus, raising of the dead) are argued to be greater and more manifest than alleged Mahometan wonders (e.g., stones dropped by birds, concealment in caves, transfer from Mecca to Jerusalem).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scrutinize miracle-claims: check whether purported marvels are truly beyond natural explanation, whether they are public/common vs private/legendary, and whether counterexamples offered by rivals are of equal weight or are explicable by natural/ordinary means.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religious truth: moral/philosophical coherence of precepts
rubrics_metrics.description: A preceptual foundation: the precepts of Christianity that align with moral and natural philosophy and are practicable (imitable) constitute evidence for its truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate a religion by whether its ethical teachings cohere with reason and moral philosophy, and whether imitation of its exemplar's life is feasible and morally exemplary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religious truth: success/propagation as arguable evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Victory and wide propagation (occupying provinces, conversions under Caesars) are adduced as arguments for a religion's truth, though the text treats this as a weaker foundation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat political success and spread as circumstantial evidence; they can support but do not conclusively prove doctrinal truth because conquest and political favour can shape religious prevalence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for authentic miracles (vs. non-miraculous reports)
rubrics_metrics.description: Not all astonishing accounts are miracles: claims such as birds dropping stones, concealment in caves, the moon being divided, or instantaneous transport require analysis; many are not miraculous (either natural, trick, or fiction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply tests: (1) is the event inherently impossible by nature? (2) is there credible public testimony? (3) are there natural explanations? Reject as miracles those that are likely natural, metaphorical, or fabricated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasons for establishment of cities: fertility and agriculture
rubrics_metrics.description: Cities arise where the land is fertile and can feed many — agricultural productivity is a prime cause of city foundation and growth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or choosing a site for settlement, prioritize availability and quality of arable land and local capacity to sustain population.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasons for establishment of cities: access to water and navigation
rubrics_metrics.description: Access to sea or navigable waters (enabling navigation and maritime agriculture) fosters very large and opulent cities (examples: Venice, Amsterdam, parts of Holland).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trade and navigation enable the convergence of merchants; when assessing urban potential, give weight to maritime access and navigable waterways.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasons for establishment of cities: defense/inexpugnable situation
rubrics_metrics.description: An inexpugnable situation — mountains, marshes, rivers or surrounding waters — makes a site's city enduring and secure (e.g., cities founded on mountains or in marsh/island contexts are hard to assault).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For long-term survival and liberty of a polity, value defensive natural features; strategic defensibility is a criterion for a lasting city.

rubrics_metrics.name: Urban scale and regional climate/conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Regional climate affects city size: in very hot regions, very large cities are often necessary because parts of the land may be sterile or produce unevenly; in extremely cold/polar regions urban density is low or impossible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factor climate and regional fertility distribution into expectations for urban scale and form; extremes (heat/cold) change settlement patterns (e.g., scattered palaces or small villages vs. dense cities).

rubrics_metrics.name: Vitruvian human body proportions
rubrics_metrics.description: Detailed canonical proportions for the human body: (examples drawn in the text) face is 1/10 of total height; distance from hairline to chin divides into thirds; nose length relates to eye length and mouth width; many specific part-to-whole ratios (e.g., palma manus = 1/18 of height, cubitus = 1/30, total corpus = 180 parts, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these numeric ratios as rules for artistic/architectural representation of the human figure and for anatomical proportional study; the treatise follows Vitruvian scheme and recommends applying these part-to-whole measures when constructing or measuring bodies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection criteria for wet-nurse/nursemaid
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose a nurse who is neither lascivious nor drunken nor sick nor depraved in morals; avoid courtesans or immoral women as wet-nurses; prefer a modest virgin of poor but respectable rearing for raising legitimate children.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the nurse's habits shape the infant's body and manners (eyes, complexion, disposition), select caregivers with sound morals and temperance. Avoid nurses with vice, illness, or extreme passions; their influences may imprint on the child.

rubrics_metrics.name: Child-rearing practices for moral and bodily formation
rubrics_metrics.description: Early education should include varied exposures, moderate nourishment, teaching of manual and intellectual arts (living in town, knowing letters, writing, arithmetic), training of the right hand, exercise and gradual introduction to necessary expenses; avoid indulgence and unnecessary money.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Raise children with measured diet, varied sensory and social experiences, instruction in 'noble arts', and disciplined habits; do not delegate exclusively to servants with bad customs; use gradual skill training to form both body and character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Household management and prevention of fraud in stewardship
rubrics_metrics.description: When supervising a child's steward or household dispenser, guard against fraud: check written receipts, compare inventories, and do not allow indefinite delays that permit excuses; small missing items can indicate greater misconduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institute checks: require written accounts, verify against peers' knowledge, limit opportunites for misappropriation, and teach the young to value necessary expenditure and not to demand or allow wasteful largesse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determinants of offspring sex (folk-medical criteria)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sex of the child is said to be influenced by heat/cold of the parents (heat favors males, cold favors females), by which parent 'dominates' the menstrual blood, and by sexual posture/side (males conceived when the man lies on the right, females when on the left). Herbal observations (e.g., 'herba mercucialis') are adduced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is presented as empirical/folk-medicine guidance: infer sex tendencies from parental constitution, seasonal/thermal qualities, and coital practices — treat with historical skepticism but note the text treats them as plausible causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parental constitution and mixture as determinants of offspring robustness
rubrics_metrics.description: Children born of stronger, mixed, or well-matched parents tend to be more robust; sparse generation (few children) is associated with stronger progeny; pure/unmixed lineages may show different traits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When accounting for variation in offspring strength and health, consider parental vitality, mixture of lines, and the frequency/intensity of generative acts; the text uses these to explain differences like gigantes/pygmaei and other human varieties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blood qualities and physiological roles (arterial vs venous distinctions)
rubrics_metrics.description: A distinction is drawn between two kinds of vessels and blood: superficial veins with tepid red blood and deeper pulsating vessels carrying yellower, hotter blood from the heart (arterial). Menstrual/parturitional blood is described as more corruptible and potent; infant blood differs from adult blood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these qualitative distinctions to explain effects (e.g., purging, temperament, disease susceptibility) and to reason about therapies such as baths or transfusions of water types; note these are pre-modern physiological criteria grounded in humoral theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respiration as a universal animal function with modality differences
rubrics_metrics.description: All animals respire in some manner: birds, reptiles, quadrupeds breathe air; fish respire by gills but some show signs of air respiration (dolphin), some creatures use both air and water (certain crabs); respiration frequency correlates with activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In anatomical and natural-philosophical accounts, determine respiration mode by observing organs and behaviours (e.g., dolphins emit voice because they breathe air). Use respiration to explain differences in animal habits and tolerances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Age and temperament influence moral character and pursuits
rubrics_metrics.description: Old men are inclined to avarice, melancholy and love of past gains; youths are lively, daring, and enjoy bodily exercises — different ages have different dominant pursuits and dispositions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or educating persons, tailor activities and instruction to age and temperament: exercise the young physically and mentally in vigorous pursuits; expect older persons to prefer conservatism and accumulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards for accepting extraordinary human forms/abilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Extraordinary human forms (giants, pygmies, people with remarkable anatomical anomalies or feats) should be accepted on the basis of measurement, credible monuments or testimony (e.g., Claudius Caesar's chronicle of Gabbarah of nine feet), and not merely on rumor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demand empirical measures and consistent testimony before admitting tales of extreme human size or abilities; compare reports to extant monuments or recorded measurements.
